units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 1
units.deva:
नमः श्री-शङ्करानन्द-गुरु-पादाम्बु-जन्मने।
सविलास-महा-मोह-ग्राह-ग्रासैक-कर्मणे॥
units.translation: Salutation to the lotus-like feet of my teacher, Śrī Śaṅkarānanda, whose work is to swallow the crocodile of great delusion and its effects.

gloss.en: to the lotus feet of Guru Śaṅkarānanda
whose sole work is to swallow great delusion with its play

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 2
units.deva:
तत्-पादाम्बु-रुह-द्वन्द्व-सेवा-निर्मल-चेतसाम्।
सुख-बोधाय तत्त्वस्य विवेदोऽयं विधीयते॥
units.translation: This discernment of reality is set forth for the clear understanding of those whose minds have been purified through service at their teacher’s two lotus feet.

gloss.en: for those whose minds are purified by service to those two lotus feet

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 3
units.deva:
शब्द-स्पर्शादयो वेद्या वैचित्र्याज् जागरे पृथक्।
ततो विभक्ता तत्-संविद् ऐक-रूप्यान् न भिद्यते॥
units.translation: The knowable (vedyas, the sense objects) beginning with sound, touch, etc. are (mistaken as) separate (from each other, i.e., are many) in waking state due to their distinguishing characteristics (vaicitrya), whereas the knower (saṃvid, the I, the consciousness) of these which is distinct from all of them does not differ (i.e., is not many) because of its singular nature (eka-rūpya).

gloss.en: because it is one in nature

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 4
units.deva:
तथा स्वप्नेऽत्र वेद्यं तु न स्थिरं जागरे स्थिरम्।
तद्-भेदोऽतस् तयोः संविद् एकरूपा न भिद्यते॥
units.translation: Similarly in the dream state. Whereas a known object was stable (sthira, remained beyond the moment) in waking, here it is unstable (only as long as its dream thought). Thus there is a difference (in nature) between them (the dream from the waking object). (But) the knower (saṃvid, in both states) having the same nature (eka-rūpā) does not differ (i.e., there is only one I, distinct from those many and different objects).

gloss.en: here the known is not stable
one in nature, does not differ

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 5
units.deva:
सुप्तोत्थितस्य सौषुप्त-तमो-बोधो भवेत् स्मृतिः।
सा चावबुद्ध-विषयाऽवबुद्धं तत् तदा तमः॥
units.translation: For the one waking from deep sleep, there is remembrance (smṛti) that (in dreamless, deep sleep) there was cognition of ignorance (tamas-bodha) in deep sleep (in the form of ‘I knew nothing,’ even time and space disappear there). A (remembrance always) has as its object a (prior) cognition. At that time (in deep sleep), that cognition is (in the form of) tamas (complete ignorance).

gloss.en: awareness of the darkness of deep sleep
has what was known as its object
what was known then was ignorance

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 6
units.deva:
स बोधो विषयाद् भिन्नो न बोधात् स्वप्न-बोधवत्।
एवं स्थान-त्रयेऽप्येका संवित् तत्वद् दिनान्तरे॥
units.translation: That cognition (bodha, the consciousness, the awareness, the I) is distinct from its object (the complete ignorance in deep sleep), but, like in dream, does not differ from itself. Thus the knower (the consciousness) remains one only in the three states (sthāna-traya, the waking, dream, and deep sleep states) in that same way (as distinct from the changing, but itself unchanging) throughout the day.

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 7
units.deva:
मासाब्द-युग-कल्पेषु गतागम्येष्वनेकधा।
नोदेति नास्तम् एत्येका संविद् एषा स्वयं-प्रभा॥
units.translation: Throughout the countless months, years, ages and world cycles, both past and future, it neither rises (udeti) nor sets (astam eti). This one consciousness (saṃvid) is self shining (svayaṃ-prabhā, and hence, self revealing).

gloss.en: through months, years, ages, and cosmic cycles
through past and future in many ways

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 8
units.deva:
इयम् आत्मा परानन्दः पर-प्रेमास्पदं यतः।
मा न भूवं हि भूयासम् इति प्रेमात्मनीक्ष्यते॥
units.translation: This (knower, consciousness) is oneself (ātman). It is ultimate fullness (para-ānanda), because it is the natural abode (āspada) of our greatest love (para-preman). Love is seen in the self as, “May I indeed never cease to be,” “May I always be.”

gloss.en: may I never cease to be
thus love is seen directed toward oneself

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 9
units.deva:
तत् प्रेमात्मार्थम् अन्यत्र नैवम् अन्यार्थम् आत्मनि।
अतस् तत् परमं तेन परमानन्दतात्मनः॥
units.translation: Only for the sake of oneself is that love (preman) directed towards another, thus love towards oneself is never for the sake of another. Therefore, that (love in oneself) is the highest. Hence the nature of the ultimate fullness (parama-ānandatā) belongs only to the self (ātman, as its abode).

gloss.en: is for the sake of the Self
the Self is supreme bliss by nature

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 10
units.deva:
इत्थं सच्-चित्-परानन्द आत्मा युक्त्या तथाविधम्।
परं ब्रह्म तयोश् चैक्यं श्रुत्यन्तेषूपदिश्यते॥
units.translation: In this way, by this logic, existence-consciousness-fullness (sat-cit-ānanda) is the nature of oneself. Similarly (as existence-consciousness-fullness) is the ultimate brahman (ultimate reality) taught in the śrutis (the Upaniṣads) as the complete identity of these two (oneself and limitless existence-consciousness-fullness).

gloss.en: the Self is existence, consciousness, and supreme bliss
the supreme Brahman is of the same nature

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 11
units.deva:
अभाने न परं प्रेम भाने न विषये स्पृहा।
अतो भानेऽप्यभाताऽसौ परमानन्दतात्मनः॥
units.translation: If the ultimate fullness nature (parama-ānandatā) of the self was not evident (a-bhāna), there would be no ultimate love. (Yet) if it was (clearly) evident, there would be no attachment (spṛhā) towards the objects of experience (apart from oneself). Therefore, even though (self) evident, it is not (clearly) evident (i.e., it is normally misplaced upon objects of desire).

gloss.en: there is no longing for objects
the Self’s nature as supreme bliss

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 12
units.deva:
अध्येतृ-वर्ग-मध्यस्थ-पुत्राध्ययन-शब्दवत्।
भानेऽप्यभानं भानस्य प्रतिबन्धेन युज्यते॥
units.translation: Like the chanting voice of one’s child amongst a group of students, even though (the ultimate fullness nature of the self) is evident, in regard to being (distinctly) evident (bhānasya prati), it is (as well) proper to take (yujyate) it as not (clearly) evident (a-bhāna), because of obstruction (pratibandha, because of its misplacement on objects of experience).

gloss.en: like the sound of one’s child reciting

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 13
units.deva:
प्रतिबन्धोऽस्ति-भातीति-व्यवहारार्ह-वस्तुनि।
तन्-निरस्य विरुद्धस्य तस्योत्पादनम् उच्यते॥
units.translation: Toward any object is applicable the experience, “It (the existence) is” and it (the awareness) is evident” (asti-bhāti), (yet) there is an obstruction said to be the rejecting of this (tan-nirasya) and imposing its opposite (experience, “I am not their existence” and “I am not their appearance”).

gloss.en: for an object fit for ordinary experience

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 14
units.deva:
तस्य हेतुः समानाभिहारः पुत्र-ध्वनि-श्रुतौ।
इहानादिर् अविद्यैव व्यामोहैक-निबन्धनम्॥
units.translation: The reason for that (obstruction) in regard to hearing the voice of one’s child is the mingling together as the same (samāna-abhihāra, with the other voices). Here, (the reason) is beginningless (uncaused) ignorance (a-vidyā, ignorance of one’s nature as the only limitless existence, consciousness). That alone is the obstruction leading to confusion (that things exist and appear independent of my existence-consciousness, i.e., that they independently exist and are not me).

gloss.en: confusion through mingling with similar sounds
is the sole basis of delusion

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 15
units.deva:
चिद्-आनन्दमय-ब्रह्म-प्रतिबिम्ब-समन्विता।
तमो-रजस्-सत्व-गुणा प्रकृतिर् द्विविधा च सा॥
units.translation: Prakṛti (mother nature) consists of the three guṇas (attributes): tamas (density, ignorance, etc.), rajas (activity, agitation, etc.), and sattva (clarity, knowledge, etc.). It is imbued with a reflection (pratibimba, semblance, appearance) of brahman consisting of consciousness-fullness. This prakṛti has two forms (as follows).

gloss.en: joined with a reflection of Brahman, whose nature is consciousness and bliss
having the qualities of tamas, rajas, and sattva

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 16
units.deva:
सत्व-शुद्ध्यविशुद्धिभ्यां मायाऽविद्ये च ते मते।
माया-बिम्बो वशी-कृत्य तां स्यात् सर्वज्ञ ईश्वरः॥
units.translation: From the perspective of its pure sattva alone, it (prakṛti) is called ‘māyā’ (appearance, in every mind, presenting a varied world). From the perspective of its impurity (a-viśuddhi, with rajas and tamas also), it is called ‘a-vidyā’ (individual ignorance, taking all these appearances as real). ‘Īśvara’ (the Lord) is the (brahman) presence (bimba) in that (sattva only aspect) māyā, controlling (vaśī-kṛtya, as pure intelligence, cosmic order) that (prakṛti), and (thus) is all-knowing (sarva-jña).

gloss.en: by purity and impurity of sattva

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 17
units.deva:
अविद्या-वशगस् त्वन्यस् तद्-वैचित्र्याद् अनेकधा।
सा कारण-शरीरं स्यात् प्राज्ञस् तत्राभिमानवान्॥
units.translation: But the other (the jīva, the individual, the brahman presence in a-vidyā) is under the spell of a-vidyā, and, because of the variety (of rajas and tamas mixtures) in that (a-vidyā) is taken as many (as a plurality of jīvas). This (a-vidyā) is the causal body (kāraṇa-śarīra), and is the one who is identified in that (causal body). That is, (having not been able to distinguish itself from its ignorant notions about itself) it is called the ‘prājña’ (the knower consciousness, and in a daily context it is the deep sleeper).* *(But contextually here, it is this knower consciousness immersed in a-vyakta, the unmanifest, ready to awaken by its karma to a continuance of its jiva-hood, its individuality, once the world of experience re-manifests.)

gloss.en: the other is subject to ignorance
the one identified with it is prājña

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 18
units.deva:
तमः-प्रधान-प्रकृतेस् तद्-भोगायेश्वराज्ञया।
वियत्-पवन-तेजो-ऽम्बु-भुवो भूतानि जज्ञिरे॥
units.translation: Per the (karma) order wielded by the Lord, for the (earned) experiences of that (jīva), from (the then unbalanced three guṇas wherein) tamas predominance of the aspects of prakṛti were born (in their subtle form) the elements (bhūtas): space (viyat, ‘reaching everywhere’, dimension), wind (pavana, movement), fire (tejas, heat and light), water (ambu, fluidity, chemical bonding remaining while in movement), and earth (bhū, solidity, granularity, gravity).

gloss.en: from prakṛti in which tamas predominates
space, air, fire, water, and earth

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 19
units.deva:
सत्वांशैः पञ्चभिस् तेषां क्रमाद् धीन्द्रिय-पञ्चकम्।
श्रोत्र-त्वग्-अक्षि-रसन-घ्राणाख्यम् उपजायते॥
units.translation: From the sattva (knowledge) aspect of each of these five (elements) are indeed born separately (kramāt – not as a whole) the five sensory organs (indriyas) called: hearing (from the sattva, knowing, aspect of the subtle element space, dimension), touching (from the sattva aspect of the subtle element wind, movement), (similarly) seeing, tasting, and smelling.

gloss.en: from the five sattva portions of those elements
called hearing, touch, sight, taste, and smell

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 20
units.deva:
तैर् अन्तः-करणं सर्वैर् वृत्ति-भेदेन तद् द्विधा।
मनो विमर्श-रूपं स्याद् बुद्धिः स्यान् निश्चयात्मिका॥
units.translation: From (the sattva aspect of) all these (elements – as a whole, not separately) is (born) the antaḥ-karaṇa (the internal organ, the mind in all its facets) with different forms and functions (vṛtti-bheda, different thoughts that make up the mind). That (internal organ) is of two types. One type is called the manas (the mind in charge of the senses) where the thoughts have the nature of vimarśa (examination, consideration, reflection, i.e., fact finding the pros and cons of what the senses present while trying to make some sense out of the data). The other type is buddhi (the intellect, the mind in charge of knowledge) where the thoughts have the nature of niścaya (ascertainment, decision, conviction).

gloss.en: manas has the nature of deliberation

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 21
units.deva:
रजोंशैः पञ्चभिस् तेषां क्रमात् कर्मेन्द्रयाणि तु।
वाक्-पाणि-पाद-पायुपस्थाभिधानानि जज्ञिरे॥
units.translation: From the rajas (activity) aspect of the five (elements) separately (kramāt – not as a whole, (Sarva Vedānta Siddhānta Sara Saṅgraha) & (Tattva Bodha)) are born the five organs of action (karmendriyas, the powers of action) called: voicing (vāc, via vocal cords, etc., from space), handling (pāṇi, via hands, etc., from wind), moving (pāda, via feet, legs, from fire), excreting (pāyu, via the anus, etc., from water), and procreating (upa-stha, via the penis, etc., from earth).

gloss.en: from the five rajas portions of those elements
called speech, hands, feet, excretion, and generation

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 22
units.deva:
तैः सर्वैः सहितैः प्राणो वृत्ति-भेदात् स पञ्चधा।
प्राणोऽपानः समानश्चोदान-व्यानौ च ते पुनः॥
units.translation: From (the rajas aspect of) all these (elements) as a whole (sahita – not separately) comes the prāṇa (life energy, animating energy), which is of five types due to different forms and functions (vṛtti-bheda) called: outward energy (prāṇa, via outward breathing, etc.), downward energy (apāna, via inward breathing, etc.), assimilating energy (samāna, via digestion, etc.), upward energy (upāna, via retching, ejecting the prāṇa from the body, etc.), and circulating energy (vyāna, via circulatory system, etc.).

gloss.en: prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 23
units.deva:
बुद्धि-कर्मेन्द्रिय-प्राण-पञ्चकैर् मनसा धिया।
शरीरं सप्त-दशभिः सूक्ष्मं तल्-लिङ्गम् उच्यते॥
units.translation: The manas (the fact gathering mind), buddhi (the intellect), along with the five each organs of sensing (five buddhi-indriyas) and of action (five karma-indriyas), plus the five prāṇas (life energies) – as seventeen make up the (jīva’s, the individual’s) subtle body (sūkṣma-śarīra), also called the liṅga-śarīra (the body where the self gets attached, is made known, and where a live individual can be inferred in an entity).

gloss.en: with intellect, organs of action, and the five vital airs
that is called the liṅga body

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 24
units.deva:
प्राज्ञस् तत्राभिमानेन तैजसत्वं प्रपद्यते।
हिरण्य-गर्भताम् ईशस् तयोर् व्यष्टि-समष्टिता॥
units.translation: Through identification there (in the subtle body that travels in and out of waking and dream experiences, as well as from the unmanifest) this prājña (the knower in deep sleep, as well as the knower in the unmanifest, ) attains taijasatva (the nature of having its mind ‘lit-up’) at its (tayoḥ) individual level (vyaṣṭhitā, awakened to the state of its mind) and the nature of the Lord in the form of Hiraṇya-garbha at its (tayoḥ) cosmic level (samaṣṭitā).

gloss.en: the Lord attains the state of Hiraṇyagarbha

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 25
units.deva:
समष्टिर् ईशः सर्वेषां स्वात्म-तादात्म्य-वेदनात्।
तद्-अभावात् ततोऽन्ये तु कथ्यन्ते व्यष्टि-संज्ञया॥
units.translation: The Lord (as Hiraṇya-garbha, the initial cosmic person) is the totality (samaṣṭi) of all this (which has becomes this universe) due to the sense of identification (tādātmya-vedana) in all of their natures, sva-ātman, their subtle bodies, (or, rather in His cosmic subtle body). The one who is other than that one, though, in the absence of that (identification in the total) they (the wise) call the individual knower (vyaṣṭi-saṃjña, who knows little, simply by this one’s identification only with this individual body, instead of with the totality).

gloss.en: the Lord is the totality of all
through recognition of identity with their own Self

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 26
units.deva:
तद्-भोगाय पुनर्-भोग्य-भोगायतन-जन्मने।
पञ्ची-करोति भगवान् प्रयेकं वियद्-आदिकम्॥
units.translation: To provide objects of experiences for those (individual subtle bodies), and provide for births into more fit receptacles of these experiences (punar-bhogya-bhoga-āyatana-janmas), the Lord (bhagavat) mixed each one (of these elements), beginning with space, five-fold*. As an example, the subtle principal of space is dimension, whereas our common parlance of experience and understanding of space is mostly the outer space beyond the atmosphere, which has relative minor percentages of movement, heat and light, liquidity, and solidity. Currently outer space is understood, per Wikipedia, as a hard vacuum containing a low density of particles, predominantly a plasma of hydrogen and helium, as well as electromagnetic radiation, magnetic fields, neutrinos, dust, and cosmic rays, and having a baseline temperature of about 2.7 °C above absolute zero temperature. Similarly, the subtle principle of wind is movement, whereas our experience and understanding of wind is the atmosphere as being predominantly movement or circulation, and relatively less amount of dimension compared to outer space, as well as of the other three elements present in the atmosphere. This is certainly a reasonably intelligent understanding of our entire universe, not displaced, though for other purposes elaborated upon by our current sciences. It’s good enough here to then understand how this universe can be completely subordinated because of its dependencies to the more unifying principles first of my mind, then the Lord’s mind [Hiraṇya-garbha], and finally the one existence-consciousness.)

gloss.en: to produce objects, enjoyment, and places of experience

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 27
units.deva:
द्विधा विधाय चैकैकं चतुर्धा प्रथमं पुनः।
स्वस्वेतर-द्वितीयांशैर् योजनात् पञ्च पञ्च ते॥
units.translation: (The five-folding to make one gross element is) proportioning into two portions and then the first portion into four portions*, so that the second (predominant) portion is (the one subtle element) itself alone and each of the other four portions are the other (subtle elements). From this combination (yogana) there are five (gross elements) each consisting of five (subtle elements, with each gross element being called its predominant subtle element component). The confusion is that dividing an element would leave a portion of itself in the first half, but, not mentioned, that half loses its element and then is replaced by quarter, at this point eighth, portions with each of the other elements. The end result would be only five gross elements of exactly half itself and one-eighth each the other four, leaving no variety within each gross element. The better understanding is to take ‘into two’ as describing a predominance of itself for each element, with the balance ‘into four’ as minority portions for the other elements. So we don’t necessarily have five unique gross elements, but a spectrum of higher and lesser predominance of dimension, movement, etc. in different locations which, through our senses, the mind then names as more or less spacious, more or less gaseous, etc.)

gloss.en: then dividing the first part into four
with the secondary portions of the other elements
thus each of the five is fivefold

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 28
units.deva:
तैर् अण्डस् तत्र भुवनं भोग्य-भोगाश्रयोद्भवः।
हिरण्य-गर्भः स्थूलेऽस्मिन् देहे वैश्वा-नरो भवेत्॥
units.translation: As these (five subtle elements) was the source (aṇḍa, the cosmic egg). In that (egg), the universe (bhuvana) arose, which then became the abode for the (earned) experiences (of the jīva, the prājña, individuals awaiting in the unmanifest for this universe to manifest, as well as the knower in deep sleep who can awaken to the day). Hiraṇya-garbha (the knower reflected in the total subtle body) is then present in this (cosmic) gross (element body, who can then be called Virāj as the knower therein).* In the (individual’s) body it would be called the vaiśvā-nara (the common-world knower, the individual who can now experience the common manifest world, who awakens to the manifest day of experiences). The answer manufactured here is directed to mature adults, but is not completely unlike the answer to children that it was a stork who brought you to us – it is what the recipient can find helpful for the time being).

gloss.en: arising as the support for objects and experience

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 29
units.deva:
तैजसा विश्वतां याता देव-तिर्यङ्-नरादयः।
ते पराग्-दर्शिनः प्रत्यक्-तत्त्व-बोध-विवर्जिताः॥
units.translation: (This same one, at the individual level) comes to be (called) the taijasas (the knowers who only light the mind within, the dreamers; the switch to plural here may be due to multiple, separate episodes of knowing different dreams before the waking day arrives) and they become known as the viśva (the pervading one, the dreamer manifesting throughout inside the dream) as a deity, animal, human, etc. (hence also the reason for the plural being used here). All of these (individual knowers: the deep sleeper, the waker, and the dreamer) experience (through the senses and mind) only the external (sense objects and thoughts in the mind) and are without true knowledge of the (knower) within (as being the same knower as Hiraṇya-garbha).

gloss.en: devoid of knowledge of the inner reality

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 30
units.deva:
नद्यां कीटा इवावर्ताद् आवर्तान्तरम् आशु ते।
व्रजन्तो जन्मनो जन्म लभन्ते नैव निर्वृतिम्॥
units.translation: These (jīvas) do action to enjoy and enjoy to do action. Like worms swiftly moving in a river from one whirlpool to another, these individuals move from birth to birth (janman), never gaining peace (nirvṛti).

gloss.en: they act for the sake of experience
and experience in order to act
they pass from birth to birth

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 31
units.deva:
सत्-कर्म-परिपाकात् ते करुणा-निधिनोद्धृताः।
प्राप्य तीर-तरु-च्छायां विश्राम्यन्ति यथा-सुखम्॥
units.translation: Due to the maturation of their good karma, a few (worms) are rescued (from the river) by someone who is a reservoir of compassion (karuṇā-nidhi). Gaining this shade of a tree on the bank, they rest in that pleasure.

gloss.en: through the ripening of good action
are lifted up by the ocean of compassion
having reached the shade of a tree on the bank

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 32
units.deva:
उपदेशम् अवाप्यैवम् आचार्यात् तत्त्व-दर्शिनः।
पञ्च-कोश-विवेकेन लभन्ते निर्वृतिं पराम्॥
units.translation: Similarly, (a few jīvas by their good karma) gain this teaching (upadeśa) from a teacher (ācārya) who knows (as clear as seeing) this truth. Through the discernment (viveka) of (the following) pañca-kośa (the five levels, where entrapment is to be avoided), they attain ultimate peace (nivṛti, release from the force of the currents of saṃsāra).

gloss.en: from a teacher who sees truth
through discernment of the five sheaths

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 33
units.deva:
अन्नं प्राणो मनो बुद्धिर् आननश्चेति पञ्च ते।
कोशास् तैर् आवृतः स्वात्मा विस्मृत्या संसृतिं व्रजेत्॥
units.translation: These five kośas (locations where one identifies with and holds on to one’s elemental gross and subtle body, literally ‘treasure chests’) are: this (body made of) food (anna), energy (prāṇa), mind (manas, the examining aspect of the mind), knowledge (buddhi, the knowing aspect of the mind, and the home of one’s ego), and pleasure (ānanda). Trapped by these as though they were one’s very self, and oblivious (to one’s true nature) they undergo (remain in) saṃsāra (cycles of rebirth).

gloss.en: food, vital energy, mind, intellect, and bliss
the Self is covered by them

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 34
units.deva:
स्यात् पञ्ची-कृत-भूतोत्थो देहः स्थूलोऽन्न-संज्ञकः।
लिङ्गे तु राजसैः प्राणैः प्राणः कर्मेन्द्रियैः सह॥
units.translation: The gross body (sthūla deha) born of the five-folded gross (the tamas aspect of the) elements (pañcī-kṛta-bhūtas, ) is known as the anna (the food body). Whereas, within the liṅga (the subtle, ) body is the prāṇa (kośa) consisting of the rajas (aspect of all the five subtle elements) in the form of the (five) prāṇas, along with the (five) karmendriyas ().

gloss.en: with vital forces born of rajas
vital function together with the organs of action

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 35
units.deva:
सात्विकैर् धीन्द्रियैः साकं विमर्शात्मा मनोमयः।
तैर् एव साकं विज्ञानमयो धीर् निश्चयात्मिका॥
units.translation: The mind having the nature of examining (vimarśa-ātman) (born) of the sātvika (subtle aspect of the five elements), along with the (five) organs of perceptual knowledge, is known as the mental (mano-maya, kośa). The intellect (dhī) having the nature of resolve, also along with those (organs of perceptual knowledge), is known as the intellectual (vijñāna-maya, kośa).

gloss.en: together with the knowledge organs born of sattva

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 36
units.deva:
कारणे सत्त्वम् आनन्दमयो मोदादि-वृत्तिभिः।
तत्-तत्-कोशैस् तु तादात्म्याद् आत्मा तत्-तन्-मयो भवेत्॥
units.translation: The sattva (aspect of all the five subtle elements) in the causal body (kāraṇa, the unmanifest basis of this universe) is with modification of moda (degrees of pleasures), etc. (i.e., priya-moda-pramoda, (Taittirīya Upaniṣad)), and is known as ānanda-maya (the kośa consisting of pleasure). Due to identification (tād-ātmya) with each one of the kośas (locations where identification mistakes are made) then the self would be assumed to have the natures of each one of them (tad-tad-maya, ‘I am skinny’, ‘I am sick’, I am unsure’, ‘I am not smart’, ‘I am not very happy’, and so on).

gloss.en: with joy and its other forms
the Self seems to take on its nature

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 37
units.deva:
अन्वय-व्यतिरेकाभ्यां पञ्च-कोश-विवेकतः।
स्वात्मानं तत उद्धृत्य परं ब्रह्म प्रपद्यते॥
units.translation: By discerning (the one essential nature) of each of the five kośas through anvaya-vyatireka (co-presence and co-absence methodology, which is discerning the essential, material or efficient cause that allows an effect to be present and without which an effect would be absent), then one draws out (of that self-kośa identification) just one’s self (as the only true nature of this identification complex) and arrives at limitless brahman (limitless reality-consciousness as my essential nature, not the limited locations it appears to be though mistaken discernment).

gloss.en: through discernment of the five sheaths
separating one’s own Self from them

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 38
units.deva:
अभाने स्थूल-देहस्य स्वप्ने यद्-भानम् आत्मनः।
सोऽन्वयो व्यतिरेकस् तद् भानेऽन्यानवभासनम्॥
units.translation: In dream (svapna), wherein there is the non-appearance (a-bhāna) of this physical body, the continued presence (anvaya) of ātman (existence-awareness, now with a dream body instead within the dream) is (said to be) the anvaya (co-presence, of the self, independent from the appearance of one’s physical body). (Whereas) the non-appearance of the physical body while that (self) is manifestly present (in dream) is (said to be) its vyatireka (co-absence, of the physical body while the self independently continues).

gloss.en: when the gross body is absent
the Self is present in dream

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 39
units.deva:
लिङ्गाभाने सुषुप्तौ स्याद् आत्मनो भानम् अन्वयः।
व्यतिरेकस् तु तद्-भाने लिङ्गस्याभानम् उच्यते॥
units.translation: (Similarly) in deep sleep (suṣupti), wherein there is the non-appearance (even) of the subtle body (liṅga, the prāṇa, manas, etc., ), the continued presence of ātman (existence-awareness, with neither a waking nor a dream body) is the anvaya. Whereas, the non-appearance of the subtle body while that (self) is manifestly present is said to be its vyatireka (co-absence, of the subtle body while the self independently continues).

gloss.en: when the subtle body is absent in deep sleep
is said to be the absence of the subtle body

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 40
units.deva:
तद्-विवेक-विविक्ताः स्युः कोशाः प्राण-मनो-धियः।
ते हि तत्र गुणावस्था-भेद-मात्रात् पृथक् कृताः॥
units.translation: Those (subtle body) kośas consisting of prāṇa, manas, and intellect (dhī) are distinguished by this discernment (viveka) from that (co-present self). In that case, they are also distinguished (from each other also) simply by the difference in their natures and their location (avasthā, i.e., separately within the subtle body and together only in waking and dream, not deep sleep).

gloss.en: of vital energy, mind, and intellect
only by differences of quality and state

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 41
units.deva:
सुषुप्त्यभाने भानं तु समाधावात्मानोऽन्वयः।
व्यतिरेकस् त्वात्म-भाने सुषुप्त्यनवभासनम्॥
units.translation: Whereas, in samādhi* (contemplation where there is only awareness that is oneself and no separation of knower-known) which is also without suṣupti (deep sleep), there is the anvaya, (continued presence, of the self, of existence-awareness alone). And the non-appearance of deep sleep (as well as of the causal ignorance of the prājña, ) while the self is manifestly present is (said to be) its vyatireka (co-absence, of the unmanifest, as well as one’s causal body without modification of moda, degrees of pleasure , while the self independently continues). When the mind in nididhyāsana eventually either drops cognizance of a separation between meditator-meditating-meditated, or comes to, at least for a time, doubtlessly appreciate the unreality of a distinction of meditator-meditating-meditated, even though they still appear in the mind, this may be called samādhi within nididhyāsana. And the Bhagavad Gītā sanctions this use of the term samādhi, (Bhagavad Gītā). Even the yoga tradition acknowledges that one arrives at samādhi through dhāraṇā and dhyāna, (Yoga Sūtras). We can take nididhyāsana, including the more general term dhyāna, as encompassing dhāraṇā, dhyāna, and samādhi, when the contemplated relates to oneself as brahman.)

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 42
units.deva:
यथा मुञ्जाद् इषीकैवम् आत्मा युक्त्या समुद्धृतः।
शरीर-त्रितयाद् धीरैः परं ब्रह्मैव जायते॥
units.translation: Like the internal pith (iṣīkā, for making the upanāyana ceremonial waistband is separated with care) from the muñja grass, so the ātman is carefully separated by the wise (dhīras) with (the help of this teaching and supporting) logic (yukti) from (the kośas of) the three bodies (the gross, subtle, and causal bodies). Then one is (as though) reborn as the ultimate brahman alone (no longer limited by these kośas).

gloss.en: as the pith is drawn from muñja grass

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 43
units.deva:
परापरात्मनोर् एवं युक्त्या संभावितैकता।
तत् त्वम् अस्यादि-वाक्यैस् सा भाग-त्यागेन लक्ष्यते॥
units.translation: In this way is manifestly taught (saṃbhāvitā) with (the help of) logic one’s identity with the para-ātman (unlimited self) from the a-para-ātman (imagined limited self, as these kośas). (Similarly) this (identity) is indicated (lakṣyate) by eliminating (unequal) aspects (bhāga-tyāga) through the (mahā-)vākyas (pithy declarations from the Upaniṣads), such as ‘tat tvam asi’ (‘that you are’), etc. (see )

gloss.en: of the higher and lower Self
by statements such as ‘That thou art’
by giving up the incompatible parts

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 44
units.deva:
जगतो यद् उपादानं मायाम् आदाय तामसीम्।
निमित्तं शुद्ध-सत्त्वां ताम् उच्यते ब्रह्म तद्-गिरा॥
units.translation: By the word ‘tad’ (‘that’) is referenced brahman which has taken on māyā through her (predominantly) tamas (darkness) aspect which would be the material cause (upādāna) of the universe and through her pure sattva (knowledge) aspect which would be the intelligent cause (nimitta, of the universe).

gloss.en: that which is the material cause
that is called Brahman by the word ‘That’

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 45
units.deva:
यदा मलिन-सत्त्वां तां काम-कर्मादि-दूषिताम्।
आदत्ते तत् परं ब्रह्म त्वं-पदेन तदोच्यते॥
units.translation: By the word ‘tvam’ (‘you’) is referenced that same ultimate brahman, whenever it has taken on (māyā’s) sattva (knowledge aspect) mixed up (malina, with rajas and tamas, and thus limited) and (thus) defiled with desires and activities (to fulfill them), etc.

gloss.en: tainted by desire, action, and the like

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 46
units.deva:
त्रितयीम् अपि तां मुक्त्वा परस्-पर-विरोधिनीम्।
अखण्डं सच्-चिद्-आनन्दं महा-वाक्येन लक्ष्यते॥
units.translation: But eliminating these three features (tāmasī māyā upādānam plus the śuddha-sattvā māyā nimittam, and malina-sattvā māyā dūṣitā) that are incompatible with each other, no distinction (between tat and tvam, the Lord and myself) is indicated by this mahā-vākya (‘tat tvam asi’), which is their (compatible nature as) existence-consciousness-fullness (sat-cit-ānanda)*. Permanency can only be brought about by knowledge, because it is factual. Nevertheless, one has to be emotionally stable for this knowledge to assimilate to the core of one’s being and not rejected because of one’s low self opinions about the body, emotions, and intellect.)

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 47
units.deva:
सोऽयम्-इत्यादि-वाक्येषु विरोधात् तद्-इदन्तयोः।
त्यागेन भागयोर् एक आश्रयो लक्ष्यते यथा॥
units.translation: The same as in declarations such as, ‘That (past location Devadatta person) is this (present Devadatta person)’, by eliminating the two (incompatible) features (bhāgayoḥ tyāgena), in the form of ‘that’ and ‘this’, then the one basis (āśraya, ‘is Devadatta’) is indicated.

gloss.en: in statements such as ‘That is this’

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 48
units.deva:
मायाऽविद्ये विहायैवम् उपाधी पर-जीवयोः।
अखण्डं सच्-चिद्-आनन्दं पर ब्रह्मैव लक्ष्यते॥
units.translation: Eliminating (negating) both māyā and a-vidya (the cosmic and the not-knowing-individual) upādhis (apparently limiting adjuncts) of the Lord and the jīva (respectively), their non-distinction (a-khaṇḍa) is indicated as brahman only, which is their (compatible nature as) existence-consciousness-fullness.

gloss.en: of the Lord and the individual

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 49
units.deva:
स-विकल्पस्य लक्ष्यत्वे लक्ष्यस्य स्याद् अवस्तुता।
निर्-विकल्पस्य लक्ष्यत्वं न दृष्टं न च सम्भवि॥
units.translation: (Objection:) If the nature of what is being indicated (lakṣyatva) is sa-vikalpa (having apparent features, the upādhis, not its real, essential nature), then the indicated lacks (independent) reality (apart from those features). But if the nature of what is being indicated is nir-vikalpa (having no apparent features), then (the indicated) is neither seen (dṛṣṭa, to the senses) nor (logically) possible (sambhavin, to the mind).

gloss.en: if it is the object indicated

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 50
units.deva:
विकल्पो निर्-विकल्पस्य स-विकल्पस्य वा भवेत्।
आद्ये व्याहतिर् अन्यत्रानवस्थाऽत्माश्रयादयः॥
units.translation: (Reply, assuming the above two objections are true:) If (brahman) having no features (nir-vikalpa) can (by the senses or mind) be figured out (vikalpa, can be featured), then this starts out as (an unresolvable) contradiction (vyāhati). If (brahman) having features can be figured out, then there will be (various logical fallacies, such as) anyatra-an-avasthā (mutual dependence, i.e., if the known features are dependent upon an unknown brahman, then the features are not fully known, and may themselves be equally unreal, if brahman happens to be unreal) or ātma-āśraya (self dependence, i.e., if brahman is completely independent from the features, then the features will tell us nothing about an unknown brahman), etc.

gloss.en: of what is distinctionless or qualified
infinite regress, self-dependence, and the like

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 51
units.deva:
इदं गुण-क्रिया-जाति-द्रव्य-सम्बन्ध-वस्तुषु।
समं तेन स्व-रूपस्य सर्वम् एतद् इतीष्यताम्॥
units.translation: This same (idaṃ samam, uncertainty would then apply) towards any object (vastu) having a quality, having an action, having a category, having a substance, and having a relationship (i.e., the relative things of the world would only be relatively known). Hence, it is instead to be understood (through the authority of the scriptural teaching) that all this (relative and thus not absolutely real universe) is (superimposed) upon my very (undismissible, definitely real) nature (sva-rūpa, by experience as existence-consciousness, and by scripture, as limitless).

gloss.en: for things with qualities, actions, kinds, substances, and relations

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 52
units.deva:
विकल्प-तद्-अभावाभ्याम् असंस्पृष्टात्म-वस्तुनि।
विकल्पितत्व-लक्ष्यत्व-सम्बन्धाद्यास् तु कल्पिताः॥
units.translation: When the reality of the self is untouched by either (the presence of superimposed) attributes or the lack of them, then the nature of being attributed, of being logically indicated, of having any relationships, etc. are all assumptions (kalpatā vṛttis, imposed by our mind on one’s self, the knower of the mind).

gloss.en: in the Self, untouched by either
attribution, indication, relation, and the rest

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 53
units.deva:
इत्थं वाक्यैस् तद्-अर्थानुसन्धानं श्रवणं भवेत्।
युक्त्या सम्भावितत्वानुसन्धानं मननं तु तत्॥
units.translation: Thus, what is called śravaṇa (listening to the teaching) involves scrutiny as to its meaning intended by these statements (mahā-vākyas). Whereas, manana (understanding) should involve scrutiny as to its validity (towards oneself and one’s life) by means of logic (yukti).

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 54
units.deva:
ताभ्यां निर्विचिकित्सेऽर्थे चेतसः स्थापितस्य यत्।
एकतानत्वम् एतद्धि निदिध्यासनम् उच्यते॥
units.translation: What indeed is called nididhyāsana (contemplation) is the abidance (eka-tānatva) of a steadied mind upon the doubtless meaning arrived at by these two (śravaṇa and manana).

gloss.en: on the meaning free from doubt
of the mind that has been settled

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 55
units.deva:
ध्यातृ-ध्याने परित्यज्य क्रमाद् ध्येयैक-गोचरम्।
निवात-दीपवच् चित्तं समाधिर् अभिधीयते॥
units.translation: In stages (kramāt, where initially one starts with a distinction of knower-knowing-known), eliminating (the notion of a distinction) as an agent and the action of meditating, where the mind, like a flame protected from the (vacillations of the) wind, has as its scope only the one dhyeya (the contemplated, self as limitless existence-consciousness, unswayed by doubts), is called samādhi (staying put only in oneself).

gloss.en: with only the object of meditation as its field
like a lamp in a windless place

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 56
units.deva:
वृत्तयस् तु तदानीम् अज्ञाता अप्यात्म-गोचराः।
स्मरणाद् अनुमीयन्ते व्युत्थितस्य समुत्थितात्॥
units.translation: Although, at that time (initially as an experience, (Yoga Sūtras) & (Yoga Sūtras), before assimilated knowledge, & (Yoga Sūtras)) this flow of thoughts, whose scope is only the self, are not (individually) known (i.e., even though they are there, they amount only to a single experiential quietude in oneself), and they, after one has arisen from being thus immersed (samutthita), are inferred to be there from a memory (of that quietude in the self, i.e., whose distinction from the quietude of deep sleep is that one entered with and emerged with a certain knowledge of oneself, unlike sleep where one starts from a forgetting of oneself).

gloss.en: having the Self as their object

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 57
units.deva:
वृत्तीनाम् अनुवृत्तिस् तु प्रयत्नात् प्रथमाद् अपि।
अदृष्टासकृद्-अभ्यास-संस्कार-सचिवाद् भवेत्॥
units.translation: The continuous flow (anuvṛtti, of thoughts on the same object during samādhi) is by previous effort (in śravaṇa, manana, and nididhyāsana to arrive at samādhi) and (then during the samādhi) by the assistance of latent tendencies (saṃskāras, in the unconscious mind, (Yoga Sūtras)) created by repeated practice and (retained) as one’s unseen (karma, even from prior births).

gloss.en: assisted by unseen impressions of repeated practice

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 58
units.deva:
यथा-दीपो-निवातस्थ इत्यादिभिर् अनेकधा।
भगवान् इमम् एवार्थम् अर्जुनाय न्यरूपयत्॥
units.translation: This very same idea, Lord (Kṛṣṇa) pointed out to Arjuna in various ways by such statements, ‘Like the (flame of an) oil lamp in a windless place’ ( (Bhagavad Gītā)).

gloss.en: by examples such as a lamp in a windless place

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 59
units.deva:
अनादाविह संसारे सञ्चिताः कर्म-कोटयः।
अनेन विलयं यान्ति शुद्धो धर्मो विवर्धते॥
units.translation: Here in beginningless saṃsāra are accumulated (sañcita, in one’s unconsciousness) countless karmas (as latent tendencies to later manifest). By this (śravaṇa, manana, and nididhyāsana, leading to samādhi) those (latent tendencies that are unhelpful, kliṣṭa, (Yoga Sūtras)) are kept in remission (vilayaṃ yānti), and there arises (to the fore) pure (helpful sattva) dharma (supporting karma).

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 60
units.deva:
धर्म-मेघम् इमं प्राहुस् समाधिं योग-वित्तमाः।
वर्षत्येष यतो धर्मामृत-धारास् सहस्रशः॥
units.translation: Experts in yoga call this samādhi a rain-cloud of dharma ( (Yoga Sūtras)), because it pours countless showers of immortal dharma (karma that relieves and helps you get out of the mortality of saṃsāra).

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 61
units.deva:
अमुना वासना-जले निःशेषं प्रविलापिते।
स-मूलोन्मूलिते पुण्य-पापाख्ये कर्म-सञ्चये॥
units.translation: By that (dharma-megha, a blessing of the teaching), one brings about the complete abatement (discount, as to not affecting one’s self), by its very root (which is ignorance of one’s real nature), of one’s accumulated (sañcaya) karma, called puṇya-pāpa (favorable and unfavorable), which (one carries around) as a pool of vāsanās (in the citta, baggage, of one’s subtle body).

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 62
units.deva:
वाक्यम् अप्रतिबद्धम् सत् प्राक् परोक्षावभासिते।
करामलकवद् बोधम् अपरोक्षं प्रसूयते॥
units.translation: The true (sat) words of the teaching (vākya), freed from obstacles (of ambiguity and doubt, through śravaṇa and manana. respectively), which previously were viewed as parokṣa (beyond the scope of one’s senses), now bears fruit (prasūyate) as direct knowledge (a-parokṣam bodham, wherein the ‘experience’ of samādhi amounts to direct evidence that action and the mind are not required for this peace in oneself that one always seeks), like āmalaka fruit (the Indian gooseberry) in the hand (is directly, not remotely, known).

gloss.en: like a fruit in the palm

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 63
units.deva:
परोक्षं ब्रह्म-विज्ञानं शाब्दं देशिक-पूर्वकम्।
बुद्धि-पूर्व-कृतं पापं कृत्स्नं दहति वह्निवत्॥
units.translation: The assimilated knowledge (vijñāna) of brahman (limitless existence-consciousness, i.e., as oneself), which was (previously) indirect (parokṣa, as belonging to the Lord) and which was introduced by a teacher (deśika-pūrva, who can only point to the truth, not ‘give’ you the truth) through words (sābda, i.e., indirectly) – now, like a fire, completely burns up the pāpa (all karma, good or bad, that kept you in cycles of rebirths) committed prior to this knowledge.

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 64
units.deva:
अपरोक्षात्म-विज्ञानं शाब्दं देशिक-पूर्वकम्।
संसार-कारणाज्ञान-तमसश् चण्ड-भास्करः॥
units.translation: The assimilated knowledge (vijñāna), having the nature of not being out of reach of one’s experience (a-parokṣa), which was introduced by a teacher (as someone required to guide and clarify your way in the scripture) through their words (sābda), like the bright light of the sun, (leads you) out of the darkness of ignorance that is the material cause of saṃsāra (unbecoming becoming).

gloss.en: the darkness of ignorance, cause of saṃsāra

units.label: Chapter 1 · Verse 65
units.deva:
इत्थं तत्त्व-विवेकं विधाय विधिवन्-मनस् समाधाय।
विगलित-संसृति-बन्धः प्राप्नोति परं पदं नरो न चिरात्॥
units.translation: Thus, one starts distinguishing through tattva-viveka (discernment of reality, from ignorance, from māyā and her effects, such as the pañca-koṣas) and begins to settle the instructed mind (in that reality). Before long, the retained notions of bondage come to an end and the person attains the ultimate abode (paraṃ padam, brahman only as oneself).

gloss.en: freed from the bond of transmigration

units.label: Chapter 2 · Verse 1
units.deva:
सद्-अद्वैतं श्रुतं यत् तत् पञ्च-भूत-विवेकतः।
बोद्धुं शक्यं ततो भूत-पञ्चकं प्रविविच्यते॥
units.translation: That non-dual Being, stated in śruti, can be known by discrimination of the five elements. Therefore the five elements are examined in detail.

gloss.en: by discrimination of the five elements

units.editionTranslation: Since that (brahman), which is said to be non-dual reality according to scripture (śruta), can be known by distinguishing (it) from the five elements (pañca-bhūta-viveka), then the nature of the five elements is now pointed out in more detail.

units.label: Chapter 2 · Verse 2
units.deva:
शब्द-स्पर्शौ रूप-रसौ गन्धो भूत-गुणा इमे।
एक-द्वि-त्रि-चतुः-पञ्च-गुणा व्योमादिषु क्रमात्॥
units.translation: Sound and touch, form and taste, smell: these are the qualities of the elements. In those beginning with space, the qualities are one, two, three, four, and five, in order.

gloss.en: having one, two, three, four, and five qualities

units.editionTranslation: The properties (guṇas, perceived by the senses) of the (gross) elements are sound (from space, as dimension, sensed by the organ of hearing through the ears), touch (from wind, movement, sensed by the organ of touch throughout the surfaces of the body), form (from fire, as heat and light, sensed by sight through the eyes), taste (from water, as liquidity, sensed by the organ of taste primarily through the tongue), and smell (from earth, as solidity, sensed by the organ of smell through the nose). These guṇas in space, etc. are accumulatively (kramāt, by five-fold physicalizing, ) one (guṇa, in space), two (guṇas, i.e., sound and touch, in wind), (similarly) three, four and five (respectively in the other three elements).

units.label: Chapter 2 · Verse 3
units.deva:
प्रति-ध्वनिर् वियच्-छब्दो वायौ बीसीति शब्दनम्।
अनुष्णा-शीत-संस्पर्शः वह्नौ भुगु-भुगु-ध्वनिः॥
units.translation: Echo is the sound of space. In wind is the sound “bīsī”; its touch is neither hot nor cold. In fire is the sound “bhugu-bhugu.”

gloss.en: touch that is neither hot nor cold

units.editionTranslation: An echo is a sound in space (viyat, dimension, properly it is that which is the medium that allows sound waves to exist and travel). In wind is sound, such as ‘bīsi’ (a whooshing soundalike, made by the movement of air in space), and touch which is (intrinsically) neither cold nor hot, i.e., has not the qualities of fire, etc.). In fire is sound, such as ‘bhugu-bhugu’ (a cracking soundalike)…

units.label: Chapter 2 · Verse 4
units.deva:
उष्णः स्पर्शः प्रभा-रूपं जले बुलु-बुलु-ध्वनिः।
शीतः स्पर्शः शुक्ल-रूपं रसो माधूर्यम् ईरितः॥
units.translation: Hot is touch; radiance is form. In water is the sound “bulu-bulu.” Cold is touch; white is form; sweetness is said to be taste.
units.editionTranslation: …Also (fire, i.e., heat and light) has (the sensed qualities) touch (from wind) and heat (from itself). In water (liquidity) is sound, such as ‘bulu-bulu’ (a gurgling soundalike), and (has a sensed) touch (from wind), a cool temperature and clear color (from fire), and produces (īrita) a refreshing taste (from itself as clean water)…

units.label: Chapter 2 · Verse 5
units.deva:
भूमौ कडकडाशब्दः काठिन्यं स्पर्श इष्यते।
नीलादिकं चित्र-रूपं मधुराम्लादिको रसः॥
units.translation: On earth is the sound “kaḍakaḍa.” Hardness is said to be touch. Blue and the like are varied forms; sweet, sour, and the like are tastes.
units.editionTranslation: …In earth (solidity) is sound, such as ‘kaḍa-kaḍā’ (a rumbling soundalike). It produces a solid touch (from contact), a varied color, such as blue, etc. (from fire via sight), a sweet, sour, etc. taste (from liquidity via the taste buds)…

units.label: Chapter 2 · Verse 6
units.deva:
सुरभी-तर-गन्धौ द्वौ गुणाः सम्यग् विवेचिताः।
श्रोत्रं त्वक् चक्षुषि जिह्वा घ्राणं चेन्द्रिय-पञ्चकम्॥
units.translation: Two smells—fragrant and other—are distinguished. Hearing, skin, eyes, tongue, and nose are the five senses.
units.editionTranslation: …Also (in earth) are pleasant and unpleasant smells (from itself). (In this way) are the qualities (of the five elements via the senses) discerned (from each other). The five sense organs are hearing (via ears), touch (via the nerved skin surfaces on and inside the body), sight (via the eyes), taste (via the taste buds on the tongue), and smell (via the nose).

units.label: Chapter 2 · Verse 7
units.deva:
कर्णादि-गोलकस्थं तच् छब्दादि-ग्राहकं क्रमात्।
सौक्ष्म्यात् कार्यानुमेयं तत् प्रायो धावेद्-बहिर्-मुखम्॥
units.translation: That [sense], dwelling in the ear and the other receptacles, grasps sound and the rest in order. Because it is subtle, it is inferred from its effects; it usually moves outward.
units.editionTranslation: Each one of these has a receptor apparatus (golakas), starting with the ears (skin, etc.), that are connected to the (sense organ) graspers (of the elements’ guṇas) starting with sound, etc. in the same order (as their predominant subtle to grosser element). Due to (the sense organs’) subtility (saukṣmya, being made only of sattva guṇa and being dependent upon their gross receptor apparatus, and thus not perceptible to these senses), each one is only inferred (by our mind, based upon their effects on the mind). Generally they (the senses) move outwards (into the world of the objects)*. *(For example, the sense of hearing perceives outwards towards the direction of the source of a sound, and sight perceives outwards to reach a perceivable form and perceives its direction and distance. Even though our modern sciences infer that the sound and light waves enter inward to the receptor apparatuses, indeed our experience is that the mind starts from you out through respective sense organ to its object.)

units.label: Chapter 2 · Verse 8
units.deva:
कदाचित् पिहिते कर्णे श्रूयते शब्द आन्तरः।
प्राण-वायौ जाठराग्नौ जल-पानेऽन्न-भक्षणे॥
units.translation: Sometimes, when the ear is closed, an inner sound is heard in the vital air, in the digestive fire, while drinking water, and while eating food.
units.editionTranslation: (Also the senses move inward, such as) when the hearing (golaka, the ears) is plugged, an interior sound is heard during breathing and during digestion (jāṭhara-agni) when drinking water or eating food…

units.label: Chapter 2 · Verse 9
units.deva:
व्यज्यन्ते ह्यान्तराः स्पर्शा मीलने चान्तरं तमः।
उद्गारे रस-गन्धौ चेत्यक्षणाम् आन्तर-ग्रहः॥
units.translation: Inner touches indeed appear; when the eyes close, inner darkness appears. At a belch, taste and smell arise. Thus the senses perceive inwardly.
units.editionTranslation: …interior sensations arise. When the eyes are closed one (‘sees’) interior darkness. When belching, there is taste and smell. Thus (iti), the senses perceive within (the body also).

units.label: Chapter 2 · Verse 10
units.deva:
पञ्चोक्त्यादान-गमन-विसर्गानन्दकाः क्रियाः।
कृषि-वाणिज्य-सेवाद्यः पञ्चस्वन्तर्भवन्ति ते॥
units.translation: The five actions are speaking, grasping, moving, releasing, and pleasure. Farming, trade, service, and the like are included among those five.
units.editionTranslation: There are (generally) five types of activities (kriyās): speaking (ukti), grasping, moving, excreting, and sexual. (All other activities, such as) agriculture, commerce, service, etc. are included within these five.

units.label: Chapter 2 · Verse 11
units.deva:
वाक्-पाणि-पाद-पायूपस्थैर् अक्षैस् तत्-क्रिया-जनिः।
मुखादि-गोलकेष्व् आस्ते तत् कर्मेन्द्रिय-पञ्चकम्॥
units.translation: Speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals are the organs that produce those actions. These five organs of action are situated in the mouth and the other receptacles.
units.editionTranslation: These activities are brought about by the (five) organs (akṣis, of action): speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals, which reside in the mouth, etc. golakas (apparatuses). These (vāk, speech, etc.) are called the five karma-indriyas (organs of action).

units.label: Chapter 2 · Verse 12
units.deva:
मनो दशेन्द्रियाध्यक्षं हृत्-पद्म-गोलके स्थितम्।
तच् चान्तःकरणं बाह्येष्वस्वातन्त्र्याद् विनेन्द्रियैः॥
units.translation: The mind, ruler of the ten senses, is situated in the receptacle of the heart-lotus. It is the inner instrument because, without the senses, it lacks independence regarding external things.
units.editionTranslation: The internal organ (antaḥ-karaṇa) is (in general called) the manas (the ‘mind’, which includes all thoughts that can be divided between examining thoughts or knowing thoughts, and those can be further divided into emotions, egos, memories, etc.). It is the overseer (adhy-akṣa) of the ten organs (of sensing and action, as part of its examining job). It is located in the lotus-like heart (hṛd, the center of the person, which is felt to be ‘working’ day and night) as its golaka (its apparatus)*. Because it lacks independence (a-svātantrya) from the (five) senses in regard to external (objects), then it is called ‘internal’. *(We may now say that the brain is the apparatus, but no arguing that if the choice is whether someone remains alive or not, it is the heart, not the brain that determines whether the subtle body remains in the body. And, one can be brain-dead, but still alive as long as the heart keeps beating.)

units.label: Chapter 2 · Verse 13
units.deva:
अक्षेष्वर्थार्पितेष्वेतद् गुण-दोष-विचारकम्।
सत्त्वं रजस् तमश् चास्य गुणा विक्रियते हि तैः॥
units.translation: When objects are placed in the senses, this [mind] judges their good and bad qualities. Sattva, rajas, and tamas are its qualities; it is indeed changed by them.
units.editionTranslation: This (mind), when present in (the field of) the senses (akṣas), examines (vicāraka) the merits and defects in regard to their contacted objects. Its (the mind’s) constituents (guṇas) by which it does its job are sattva, rajas, and tamas.

units.label: Chapter 2 · Verse 14
units.deva:
वैराग्यं क्षान्तिर् औदार्यम् इत्याद्याः सत्त्व-सम्भवाः।
काम-क्रोधौ लोभ-यत्नावित्याद्या रजसोत्थिताः॥
units.translation: Dispassion, patience, generosity, and the like arise from sattva. Desire, anger, greed, effort, and the like arise from rajas.
units.editionTranslation: The (mind’s sense of) non-attachment, accommodation, generousness, and so on are (thoughts) born of (predominance of) sattva (knowledge, objective reality). Requiring and anger, greed and contrivance, and so on arise from (predominance of) rajas (activity, clouded thinking).

units.label: Chapter 2 · Verse 15
units.deva:
आलस्य-भ्रान्ति-तन्द्राद्या विकारास् तमसोत्थिताः।
सात्त्विकैः पुण्य-निष्पत्तिः पापोत्पत्तिश्च राजसैः॥
units.translation: Laziness, confusion, drowsiness, and the like are changes arising from tamas. Merit arises from sattvic states, and demerit arises from rajasic states.
units.editionTranslation: Lethargy, confusion, drowsiness, and so on arrive from (predominance of) tamas (darkness, lack of critical thinking). By sāttvika (thoughts) there arises puṇya (lasting karma merit). By rājasa (thoughts) there arises pāpa (lasting karma demerit).

units.label: Chapter 2 · Verse 16
units.deva:
तामसैर् नोभयं किन्तु वृथायुः-क्षपणं भवेत्।
अत्राहं-प्रत्ययी कर्तेत्येवं लोक-व्यवस्थितिः॥
units.translation: From tamasic states, neither [merit nor demerit] results; rather, life would be wasted in vain. Here, the one with the “I”-notion is the doer; this is how worldly order is arranged.
units.editionTranslation: By tāmasa (thoughts) there is neither of these (karma merit or demerit), rather there would only be spending life’s energy idly. Among these (thoughts of the mind), any one that also includes a notion of ‘I’ (ahaṃ-pratyayin, such as ‘My non-attachment’, ‘I am desirous’, etc.) is called the kartā (the doer, doership). Thus, is our worldly experience (of how the mind reacts through its constituent nature).

units.label: Chapter 2 · Verse 17
units.deva:
स्पष्ट-शब्दादि-युक्तेषु भौतिकत्वम् अतिस्फुटम्।
अक्षादावपि तत्-शास्त्र-युक्तिभ्याम् अवधार्यताम्॥
units.translation: The elemental nature is very clear in things that have clear sound and the rest. Even for the senses and the rest, it should be ascertained through scripture and reasoning.

gloss.en: in the senses and the rest

units.editionTranslation: Concerning these (sense experiences via the thoughts of the mind) consisting of sound, etc., the nature of their also being only products of the (five subtle) elements (bhautikatva) is not clearly known (due to their subtility (saukṣmya, , as well as due to our identification with the mind and senses that we don’t recognize them as objects also). However, even in regard to the senses, etc. (mind, intellect, ego), there is ascertainment (of their elemental nature) through the scripture (śāstra) and (supporting) logic (yukti) on this topic.
units.iast:
spaṣṭa-śabdādi-yukteṣu bhautikatvam atisphuṭam ।
akṣādāv api tac-chāstra-yuktibhyām avadhāryatām ॥

units.label: Chapter 2 · Verse 18
units.deva:
एकादशेन्द्रियैर् युक्त्या शास्त्रेणाप्यवगम्यते।
यावत् किंचिद् भवेद् एतद् इदं-शब्दोदितं जगत्॥
units.translation: Whatever in this world is called “this” is understood through the eleven organs, reasoning, and scripture.
units.editionTranslation: Whatever is experienced through the eleven organs (of the five senses, of the five actions, and the one internal organ), plus that understood through logic and the scripture (as the third separate pramāṇa, means of knowledge, (Yoga Sūtras)), is this world referred to as idam (‘this’, in the following quote).
units.iast:
ekādaśendriyair yuktyā śāstreṇāpy avagamyate ।
yāvat kiṃcid bhaved etad idaṃ-śabdoditaṃ jagat ॥

units.label: Chapter 2 · Verse 19
units.deva:
इदं सर्वं पुरा सृष्टेर् एकम् एवाद्वितीयकम्।
सद् एवासीन् नाम-रूपे नास्ताम् इत्यारुणेर् वचः॥
units.translation: Before creation, all this was Existence alone, one, and without a second. Name and form were not. This is the statement of Āruṇi.
units.editionTranslation: Uddālaka Āruṇi taught (to Śvetaketu, in the sixth chapter of Chāndogya Upaniṣad, , (Chāndogya Upaniṣad)) that before all “this” (idam) manifest universe (śṛṣṭi) “there was one reality only without a second” (ekam eva sad eva a-dvitīyam āsīt); there was no “name or form” (nāma-rūpa).

units.label: Chapter 2 · Verse 20
units.deva:
वृक्षस्य स्वगतो भेदः पत्र-पुष्प-फलादिभिः।
वृक्षान्तरात् सजातीयो विजातीयः शिलादितः॥
units.translation: A tree’s difference within itself is through leaves, flowers, fruits, and the like; from another tree it differs as one of the same kind, and from a stone and the like as a different kind.

gloss.en: from a stone and the like

units.editionTranslation: A difference (bheda, to make a second, dvitīya, a separate name and form) is (of three types): sva-gata (present within itself), such as of a tree by its leaves, flowers, fruits, etc.; sa-jātīya (between its same class), such as (of one tree) from another tree; and vi-jātīya (apart from another class), such as (of a tree) from a rock, etc.

units.label: Chapter 2 · Verse 21
units.deva:
तथा सद्-वस्तुनो भेद-त्रयं प्राप्तं निवार्यते।
ऐक्यावधारण-द्वैत-प्रतिषेधैस् त्रिभिः क्रमात्॥
units.translation: In the same way, the three differences that might apply to Being are removed in order by the three: oneness, restriction, and denial of duality.
units.editionTranslation: In that way, the prospect that this entity called sat (reality itself) has any of these three differences (from within, between, and apart) is warded off in order by the three (words “one only without-a-second”: eka, eva, a-dvitīya, ) which express oneness (aikya, ‘eka’, no differentiation within itself), restriction (avadhāraṇa, ‘eva’, no differentiation from a similar), and denial of a second thing (dvaita-pratiṣedha, ‘a-dvitīya’, no differentiation from a dissimilar).

units.label: Chapter 2 · Verse 22
units.deva:
सतो नावयवाः शङ्क्यास् तद्-अंशस्यानिरूपणात्।
नाम-रूपे न तस्यांशौ तयोर् अद्याप्यनुद्भवात्॥
units.translation: No parts of Being are to be assumed, because its parts cannot be established. Name and form are not its two parts, because those two have not yet arisen.
units.editionTranslation: That reality (sat, brahman) could not possibly have had parts, since there was no discerning of such parts. Names and forms (nāma-rūpa) are not its parts, since before those (names and forms, before this manifest universe those) had not yet arisen.

units.label: Chapter 2 · Verse 23
units.deva:
नाम-रूपोद्भवस्यैव सृष्टित्वात् सृष्टितः पुरा।
न तयोरुद्भवस्तस्मात् सन्निरंशं यथा वियत्॥
units.translation: Because creation is only the arising of name and form, those two had not arisen before creation. Therefore Being is partless, like space.

gloss.en: of the arising of name and form

units.editionTranslation: Since manifestation is only the arising of names and forms, then before manifestation these two would not have yet arisen. Therefore, this reality (before creation) was partless, just like space (at the start of manifestation, before the other great elements).
units.iast:
nāma-rūpodbhavasyaiva sṛṣṭitvāt sṛṣṭitaḥ purā ।
na tayorudbhavas tasmāt san niraṃśaṃ yathā viyat ॥

units.label: Chapter 2 · Verse 24
units.deva:
सद्-अन्तरं सजातीयं न वैलक्षण्य-वर्जनात्।
नाम-रूपोपाधि-भेदं विना नैव सतो भिदा॥
units.translation: There is no other Being of the same kind, because it has no distinguishing feature. Without the distinction of name and form as limiting adjuncts, Being has no division.

gloss.en: distinction of name and form as limiting adjuncts

units.editionTranslation: Since differentiation (vailakṣaṇya) was lacking, there could have been no similarity (sa-jātīya) with another reality (i.e., a class of the same kind of realities). Difference (bheda) is due to the upādhi (limiting adjunct) of names and forms. Without (those), reality cannot have a difference (to be multiple realities).

units.label: Chapter 2 · Verse 25
units.deva:
विजातीयम् असत् तत् तु न खल्वस्तीति गम्यते।
नास्यातः प्रतियोगित्वं विजातीयाद् भिदा कुतः॥
units.translation: Non-being does not exist as something of a different kind. It is understood that it is no opposite of Being; how, then, could there be a difference of another kind?
units.editionTranslation: Nor could one conceive of non-reality (a-sat) as vijātīya (belonging to a different class from reality). Since nothing can have opposition (pratiyogin) from this (reality, i.e., ‘existence’ includes everything that possibly or impossibly was, is, or will be, even the notion that there is a non-existence exists), then how could there be a difference (from reality) as a different class?

units.label: Chapter 2 · Verse 26
units.deva:
एकम् एवाद्वितीयं सत् सिद्धम् अत्र तु केचन।
विह्वला असद् एवेदं पुरासीद् इत्यावर्णयन्॥
units.translation: Being is established as one alone, without a second. But some, bewildered, describe this as: “Before, this was non-being alone.”
units.editionTranslation: That reality (sat) is one only without a second has been established. But, in regard to this, some are confused (vihvalas, vyākulas, such as Vaināśikas, Buddhist Nihilists) choosing to say that there was non-reality (a-sat, non-existence) before (the manifestation of the universe).

units.label: Chapter 2 · Verse 27
units.deva:
मग्नस्याब्धौ यथाक्षाणि विह्वलानि तथास्य धीः।
अखण्डैक-रसं श्रुत्वा निष्प्रचारा बिभेत्यतः॥
units.translation: Just as the senses of one sunk in the ocean are bewildered, so his mind, on hearing of the one undivided essence, becomes inactive and is afraid.
units.editionTranslation: Like sinking into the ocean (with nothing but water all around) one’s senses and mind are bewildered, upon hearing that reality is one without divisions (to cling to). These individuals have thus become stunned and very fearful.

units.label: Chapter 2 · Verse 28
units.deva:
गौडाचार्या निर्विकल्पे समाधावन्य-योगिनाम्।
साकार-ध्यान-निष्ठानाम् अत्यन्तं भयमूचिरे॥
units.translation: The Gauḍācārya spoke of great fear among other yogis devoted to meditation on form, in non-conceptual samādhi.
units.editionTranslation: The teacher Gauḍa-pāda talked about the great fear of some yogins ( (Māṇḍūkya Up. Kārikā)) who are dedicated only to brahman with a form (sākāra) when their contemplation becomes free of (mental) divisions.
units.iast:
gauḍācāryā nirvikalpe samādhāv anyayoginām ।
sākāra-dhyāna-niṣṭhānām atyantaṃ bhayam ūcire ॥

units.label: Chapter 2 · Verse 29
units.deva:
अस्पर्श-योगो नामैष दुर्दर्शः सर्व-योगिभिः।
योगिनो बिभ्यति ह्य्-अस्माद् अभये भय-दर्शिनः॥
units.translation: This is called asparśa-yoga; it is hard for all yogis to perceive. Indeed, yogis fear it, seeing fear in the fearless.
units.editionTranslation: All such yogins, who find what is called a-sparśa (without a sense or mental contact) yoga difficult to conceive, are afraid of it, seeing fear in the fearless.

units.label: Chapter 2 · Verse 30
units.deva:
भगवत्-पूज्य-पादाश्च शुष्क-तर्क-पटून् अमून्।
आहुर् माध्यमिकान् भ्रान्तान् अचिन्त्येऽस्मिन् सद्-आत्मनि॥
units.translation: Bhagavatpāda calls these Mādhyamikas, skilled in dry reasoning, confused about this inconceivable true Self.
units.editionTranslation: The highly respected Bhagavat-pāda (Śaṅkara) calls the Mādhyamikas (Buddhists) who only have dry logic (lacking the Veda as the proper means of knowledge here) as confused regarding this reality-self which (as the witness) cannot be an object of thought.

units.label: Chapter 2 · Verse 31
units.deva:
अनादृत्य श्रुतिं मौर्ख्याद् इमे बौद्धास्तपस्विनः।
आपेदिरे निरात्मत्वम् अनुमानैक-चक्षुषः॥
units.translation: These Buddhist ascetics, through confusion, disregarded śruti and reached the view that there is no Self, seeing through inference alone.

gloss.en: the view that there is no Self
having inference as their only eye

units.editionTranslation: These Buddhists, (seemly) out of dumbness (lack of a proper means of knowledge here) disregard the scripture (śruti, teachings) and remain in darkness. As they only look through logic, they arrive at the conclusion that they themselves are nothing (nir-ātmatva).

units.label: Chapter 2 · Verse 32
units.deva:
शून्यम् आसीद् इति ब्रूषे सद्-योगं वा सद्-आत्मताम्।
शून्यस्य न तु तद्-युक्तम् उभयं व्याहतत्वतः॥
units.translation: You say, “Nothing was.” Do you mean that nothing is joined to Being, or that it is Being? Neither claim fits nothingness, because both are contradictory.
units.editionTranslation: When you (Buddhists) say śūnya (nothingness) existed, did you mean that it has existence (sat-yoga) or that it is existence (sat-ātmatā)? In either case, nothingness cannot have any such association with existence, because both non-existence and existence are contradictory (to each other, but if they mean the same thing to you then you are simply naming existence as ‘śūnya’).

units.label: Chapter 2 · Verse 33
units.deva:
न युक्तस् तमसा सूर्यो नापि चासौ तमोमयः।
सच्-छून्ययोर् विरोधित्वाच् छून्यम् आसीत् कथं वद॥
units.translation: The sun is not joined with darkness, nor is it made of darkness. Since Being and non-being are opposed, how can you say that non-being was?
units.editionTranslation: The sun cannot be attributed with darkness, nor does it consist of darkness. As existence and non-existence are (naturally) contradictory, how could you say non-existence existed (before creation)?

units.label: Chapter 2 · Verse 34
units.deva:
वियद्-आदेर् नाम-रूपे मायया सुविकल्पिते।
शून्यस्य नाम-रूपे च तथा चेज् जीव्यतां चिरम्॥
units.translation: Name and form beginning with space are imagined in Being by māyā. If name and form are likewise [imagined] in nothingness, then live long!
units.editionTranslation: (The Buddhist says:) If (for you Vedāntins) the names and forms beginning with the element space, etcetera are completely imposed (on existence) by (the inexplicable magic of) māyā, then similarly (for us Buddhists) these are simply names and forms of non-existence (śūnya, imposed, produced, by māyā). (We reply:) May you live long! (i.e., you either are talking meaninglessly or at best not disputing us, since you are accepting a thing called ‘śūnya’ that has names and forms imposed on it).

units.label: Chapter 2 · Verse 35
units.deva:
सतोऽपि नाम-रूपे द्वे कल्पिते चेत् तदा वद।
कुत्रेति निरधिष्ठानो न भ्रमः क्वचित् ईक्ष्यते॥
units.translation: If name and form are imagined even in Being, then say where. An illusion is never seen anywhere without a basis.
units.editionTranslation: You may say that both names and forms of reality are both imposed (by māyā upon non-existence), but an illusion (bhrama) is never seen anywhere without a substratum (e.g., mirage water requires a certain surface condition viewed at a certain angle; a phantom snake requires a crack on the ground, a rope, etc. in a darkened area by one who would suspect a snake could be there).

units.label: Chapter 2 · Verse 36
units.deva:
सद् आसीद् इति शब्दार्थ-भेदे वैगुण्यम् आपतेत्।
अभेदे पुनर् उक्तिः स्यान् मैवं लोके तथेक्षणात्॥
units.translation: If the words “Being” and “was” have different meanings, a defect follows. If they have the same meaning, it would be repetition. Do not say this, for such usage is seen in the world.

gloss.en: if the word and meaning differ

units.editionTranslation: (Objection:) The (Veda text’s) two words ‘sat’ ‘āsīt’ (‘reality was’) either separately refer to two different entities (śabdārthas, hence there is duality), or the expression refers to no difference (a-bheda, and hence is meaningless tautology, like ‘one is one’). (Reply:) It should not be like that, since we see such expressions in common usage.

units.label: Chapter 2 · Verse 37
units.deva:
कर्तव्यं कुरुते वाक्यं ब्रूते धार्यस्य धारणम्।
इत्यादि-वासनाविष्टं प्रत्यासीत् सद् इतीरणम्॥
units.translation: “One does what must be done,” “one speaks,” and “one carries what must be carried”: for someone filled with habits of such speech, the expression “Being was” is familiar.
units.editionTranslation: ‘A deed is done,’ ‘A speech is spoken,’ ‘A burden is borne’ – towards one who is accustomed to such expressions, the verb ‘was’ (in ‘sat āsīt’) expresses being (sat).

units.label: Chapter 2 · Verse 38
units.deva:
कालाभावे पुरेत्युक्तिः काल-वासनया युतम्।
शिष्यं प्रत्येव तेनात्र द्वितीयं नहि शङ्क्यते॥
units.translation: The word “before,” where there is no time, is used for the student who has a habit of time; therefore no second thing is to be suspected here.
units.editionTranslation: The expression ‘before’ (purā, agre) in regard to (‘before creation’) which lacks time is directed toward a student accustomed to temporal thinking, and this usage (by the teacher) here does not intend duality (existence plus time).

units.label: Chapter 2 · Verse 39
units.deva:
चोद्यं वा परिहारो वा क्रियतां द्वैत-भाषया।
अद्वैत-भाषया चोद्यं नास्ति नापि तद्-उत्तरम्॥
units.translation: Let a question or its answer be made in dualistic speech. In non-dual speech there is no question, nor its answer.
units.editionTranslation: A question (codya, pūrva-pakṣa) and its reply arise within our duality accustomed language (within nāma-rūpa, names and forms). Within a (supposed) non-duality (or non-existent) language, there can be no question or its response.

units.label: Chapter 2 · Verse 40
units.deva:
तदा स्तिमित-गम्भीरं न तेजो न तमस्ततम्।
अनाख्यम् अनभिव्यक्तं सत् किञ्चिद् अवशिष्यते॥
units.translation: Then, still and deep, with neither light nor darkness spread out, some nameless, unmanifest Being remains.
units.editionTranslation: At that time (before creation) a ‘steady depth’ (‘gambhīra’,* a-dvaita vastu) pervaded without any tejas or tamas (opposition guṇas, light-dark, movement-stasis), nor name or manifest form apart from this reality (sat). Non-being then existed not nor being: There was no air, nor sky that is beyond it. What was concealed? Wherein? In whose protection? And was there deep (gambhīra) unfathomable water?(1) Death then existed not nor life immortal; Of neither night nor day was any token. By its inherent force the One breathed windless: No other thing than that beyond existed.(2) Darkness there was at first by darkness hidden; Without distinctive marks, this all was water. That which, becoming, by the void was covered. That One by force of heat came into being.(3) Desire entered the One in the beginning: It was the earliest seed, of thought the product. The sages searching in their hearts with wisdom, Found out the bond of being in non-being.(4) Their ray extended light across the darkness: But was the One above or was it under? Creative force was there, and fertile power: Below was energy, above was impulse.(5) Who knows for certain? Who shall here declare it? Whence was it born, and whence came this creation? The gods were born after this world's creation: Then who can know from whence it has arisen?(6) None knows whence creation has arisen; And whether he has or has not produced it: He who surveys it in the highest heaven, He only knows, or haply he may know not.(7)

units.label: Chapter 2 · Verse 41
units.deva:
ननु भूम्यादिकं मा भूत् परमाण्वन्त-नाशतः।
कथं ते वियतोऽसत्त्वं बुद्धिम् आरोहतीति चेत्॥
units.translation: “Let earth and the rest be absent, dissolved down to atoms. How can the non-being of space enter your understanding?”—if this is asked.

gloss.en: because of dissolution down to atoms

units.editionTranslation: Question (nanu): Upon dissolution all the way to the atomic elements (paramāṇus) then the earth, etcetera may cease to exist, but how can I arrive at a notion that space (ākāśa) itself has no existence?

units.label: Chapter 2 · Verse 42
units.deva:
अत्यन्तं निर्जगद् व्योम यथा ते बुद्धिम् आश्रितम्।
तथैव सन् निराकाशं कुतो नाश्रयते मतिम्॥
units.translation: Just as space completely without a world is accepted in your understanding, so why does Being without space not take hold of the mind?
units.editionTranslation: If in fact you can have such an abiding knowledge that there is a space completely without a universe (of names and forms), then why can't you abide in a idea that reality (sat) can be without space?

units.label: Chapter 2 · Verse 43
units.deva:
निर्जगद् व्योम दृष्टं चेत् प्रकाश-तमसी विना।
क्व दृष्टं किंच ते पक्षे न प्रत्यक्षं वियत् खलु॥
units.translation: If space without a world is seen apart from light and darkness, where is it seen? And in your view, space itself is not directly perceived.
units.editionTranslation: If you can perceive a space without a universe, then in that case, without (the contrast of) light and dark, where could you possibly perceive (a universe-less space)? Moreover, space is indeed unseen (na pratyakṣa, is not in fact an object of the eye).

units.label: Chapter 2 · Verse 44
units.deva:
सद् वस्तु शुद्धं त्वस्माभिर् निश्चितैर् अनुभूयते।
तूष्णीं स्थितौ न शून्यत्वं शून्य-बुद्धेश्च वर्जनात्॥
units.translation: The pure reality of Being is experienced by us who are certain. When [the mind] is quiet, it is not nothingness, because the thought of nothingness is absent.
units.editionTranslation: Whereas, reality (sat, brahman) is pure existence (vastu) experienced (anu-bhūyate, literally ‘being in keeping with’) by all of us very clearly. When (the mind) remains quiet, we do not experience nothing, because there is no thought of a nothing (śūnya, at that time).

units.label: Chapter 2 · Verse 45
units.deva:
सद्-बुद्धिर् अपि चेन् नास्ति मास्त्वस्य स्व-प्रभत्वतः।
निर्मनस्कत्व-साक्षित्वात् सन्-मात्रं सुगमं नृणाम्॥
units.translation: Even if the thought of Being is absent, let it be absent, because Being is self-luminous. Because it witnesses the absence of mind, mere Being is easy for people [to know].
units.editionTranslation: (Objection:) But neither do we have a thought of existence (at that quiet time). (Reply:) Let that thought not be there, because existence is self-revealing (sva-prabhatva) and because it is the witness (sākṣitva) of the lack of thoughts (at that time). Pure existence is easy to recognize for everyone (as everyone is effortlessly always shining and witnessing whatever is there or not in their mind – a quiet mind is just an aid to confirm this teaching that it is you alone who is shining and witnessing, not any of these objects witnessed).

units.label: Chapter 2 · Verse 46
units.deva:
मनो-जृम्भण-राहिते यथा साक्षी निराकुलः।
माया-जृम्भणतः पूर्वं सत् तथैव निराकुलम्॥
units.translation: When the mind is not opening up (to an external world) then the witness (the existence of oneself) appears to be without problems (nir-ākula). Similarly (as it is now, so it was then), before the opening up (of the universe by) māyā, reality (sat) was unruffled.

gloss.en: when the mind's expansion is absent

units.label: Chapter 2 · Verse 47
units.deva:
निस्तत्वा कार्य-गम्यास्य शक्तिर् मायाऽग्नि-शक्तिवत्।
न हि शक्तिः क्वचित् कैश्चिद् बुध्यते कार्यतः पुरा॥
units.translation: Apart (nis-ta-tvā, pṛthak) from manifesting its effects, māyā is (only inferred to exist within reality as) a śakti (power, to manifest the varieties of nature from the one reality), like the power of fire (to burn only is known by its perceived effects). Because, no one knows any power exists somewhere, before its effects (are noticed).

gloss.en: of this, knowable through its effects

units.label: Chapter 2 · Verse 48
units.deva:
न सद्-वस्तु सतः शक्तिर् न हि वह्नेः स्व-शक्तिता।
सद्-विलक्षणतायां तु शक्तेर् किं तत्त्वम् उच्यताम्॥
units.translation: The power (śakti, māyā) of reality is not the reality itself. Nor can a power exist by itself (like) fire’s (power to burn does not exist apart from fire itself). If (this power, māyā) exists apart from reality, what could one say is its nature?

units.label: Chapter 2 · Verse 49
units.deva:
शून्यत्वम् इति चेच् छून्यं माया-कार्यम् इतीरितम्।
न शून्यं नापि सद् यादृक् तादृक् तत्वम् इहेष्यताम्॥
units.translation: If (you say the power, māyā) is the nature of non-existence (śūnyatva), (then this contradicts) what you said before that it is an effect of māyā (). (Māyā) is neither non-existence (śūnya) nor reality itself (sat) – whatever that is (yādṛk, neither sat nor a-sat), that (tādṛk) has to be considered its (māyā’s) nature (tatva = tattva, (Sanskrit Grammar)).

units.label: Chapter 2 · Verse 50
units.deva:
नासद् आसीन् नो सद् आसीत् तदानीं किंत्वभूत् तमः।
सद्-योगात् तमसः सत्त्वं न स्वतस् तन्-निषेधनात्॥
units.translation: (Hence it was said in Ṛg Veda, ) There was neither a-sat nor sat at that time (before creation), but there was tamas (darkness, which was what māyā is before creation, ). Existence (‘was’) is attributed to tamas (that darkness) due to its association with (i.e., appearance within) existence (sat), not due to itself alone, since (existence) is denied to it (in that Ṛg Veda hymn).

units.label: Chapter 2 · Verse 51
units.deva:
अत एव द्वितीयतं शून्यवन् न हि गण्यते।
न लोके चैत्र-तच्-छक्त्योर् जीवितं लिख्यते पृथक्॥
units.translation: Thus, like śūnya, (māyā) cannot count as a second entity (from existence, sat). In the world, an able person and his ability cannot be portrayed to live apart from each other.

units.label: Chapter 2 · Verse 52
units.deva:
शक्त्याधिक्ये जीवितं चेत् वर्धते तत्र वृद्धि-कृत्।
न शक्तिः किन्तु तत्-कार्यं युद्ध-कृष्यादिकं तथा॥
units.translation: If one’s life lengthens when one’s power increases, in that case, the act of ageing is not itself the power (to live, one’s prāṇa) but an effect of that power, such as making war or going agriculture, etcetera (are possible effects of one’s power to live). (Similarly, although māyā, the manifestation power of existence, is not an addition to that sat, the universe consists of separate effects, which do vary, of that non-addition māyā.)

units.label: Chapter 2 · Verse 53
units.deva:
सर्वथा शक्ति-मात्रस्य न पृथक् गणना क्वचित्।
शक्ति-कार्यं तु नैवास्ति द्वितीयं शङ्क्यते कथम्॥
units.translation: Everywhere, a śakti (any subtle power) itself cannot count as being separate (from that existence, or whether an element, a person or the Lord) in which it manifests, and any effect of that śakti is not itself (the śakti).
